{{Short description|Pre-modern immigrants to Japan}}
[[File:Takamat1.jpg|thumb|A mural of women in [[Goguryeo]]-style clothing on the western wall of the [[Takamatsuzuka Tomb]] ([[Kofun]]), believed to be depicting Toraijin from Goguryeo during the Asuka period.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2022-04-01 |title=高松塚・高句麗壁画の共通性 |trans-title=Takamatsuzuka Tomb・Goguryeo Tomb mural commonality |url=https://gendai.media/articles/-/93945 |access-date= |website=現代ビジネス |publisher=[[Shūkan Gendai]] |language=ja}}</ref>]]
'''Toraijin''' ({{langx|ja|渡来人, とらいじん}}) refers to the ancient people who migrated to the Japanese archipelago, as well as their naturalized descendants.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |script-title=ja:渡来人 |url=https://www.asuka-tobira.com/toraijin/toraijin.htm |access-date=2023-01-26 |website=www.asuka-tobira.com |language=ja}}</ref><ref name=":1">{{Cite web |last=第２版,世界大百科事典内言及 |first=日本大百科全書(ニッポニカ),ブリタニカ国際大百科事典 小項目事典,旺文社日本史事典 三訂版,百科事典マイペディア,デジタル大辞泉,精選版 日本国語大辞典,世界大百科事典 |title=渡来人(とらいじん)とは？ 意味や使い方 |url=https://kotobank.jp/word/%E6%B8%A1%E6%9D%A5%E4%BA%BA-585287 |access-date=2023-02-06 |website=コトバンク |language=ja}}</ref> Up until the 1960s, these people were commonly called the "Kikajin ({{langx|ja|帰化人, きかじん}})", meaning "naturalized people", but beginning in the 1970s, the term was replaced by "Toraijin", meaning "people who have crossed over" as not all those who came to Japan became naturalized.<ref name=":3" />

They arrived in Japan as early as the [[Jōmon period]] or [[Yayoi period]], and their arrival became more significant from the end of the 4th century ([[Kofun period]]) to the late 7th century ([[Asuka period]]). During these periods, they introduced [[Confucianism]], [[Buddhism]], [[Chinese characters]] ([[Kanbun]]/[[Kanji]]), [[Kampo|medicine]], [[lunar calendar]], and cultural practices such as [[Sue pottery|Sue ware]] production and weaving to Japan. They were favored by the [[Yamato Kingship|Yamato Imperial Court]], and many were appointed to government positions.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":0" />

== Overview ==
Historical records and archaeological data provide strong support for continued population movements from the continent to the Japanese archipelago via the southern [[Korean Peninsula]] from 800&nbsp;BCE to 600&nbsp;CE.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Mizoguchi |first=Koji |title=The archaeology of Japan: from the earliest rice farming villages to the rise of the state |date=2013 |publisher=Cambridge University press |isbn=978-0-521-88490-7 |series=Cambridge world archaeology |location=Cambridge}}</ref><ref name=":3">{{Cite book |last1=Rhee |first1=Song Nai |title=Archaeology and history of Toraijin: human, technological, and cultural flow from the Korean peninsula to the Japanese archipelago c. 800 BC-AD 600 |last2=Aikens |first2=C. Melvin |last3=Barnes |first3=Gina Lee |date=2022 |publisher=Archaeopress Archaeology |isbn=978-1-78969-966-1 |location=Oxford}}</ref> The Toraijin arrived in the [[Japanese archipelago|archipelago]] in multiples waves.

In the initial wave starting approximately three thousand years ago, where 20th century anthropologists such as [[Torii Ryūzō]] stated that "the Stone Age in Japan and that in Korea are very similar. The similarities are so outstanding that we can say their relationship was like that of cousins, if not of a parent and child, or siblings" in his book {{Nihongo3|''Japan before History''|有史以前の日本|Yūshi izen no Nihon}},<ref>{{Cite book |last=Torii |first=Ryūzō |title=有史以前の日本 |year=1925 |pages=382 |language=ja |trans-title=Japan before History}}</ref> highlighting a close connection between the Japanese and the Koreans even during the [[Prehistory|prehistoric]] periods due to the major overlap of immigrants.<gallery>
File:Example of a southern-style dolmen at Ganghwa Island.jpg|A Stone Age [[dolmen]] at [[Ganghwa Island]], South Korea.
File:Dolmen in Korea.png|40,000 dolmens distributed in [[Korea]] which account for approximately 40% of the world's total.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Jr |first=John M. Jensen |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=EfxiCAAAQBAJ&q=dolmen+in+korea+40%25&pg=PA276 |title=Earth Epochs: Cataclysms across the Holocene |date=2015 |publisher=John Jensen |language=en}}</ref>
File:Dolmen in Japan and Jeju.png|Dolmens found in [[Jeju Island]] and northern [[Kyushu]] (Japan).<ref>{{Cite book |last=支石墓 |title=日本国語大辞典 |publisher=小学館 |language=ja}}</ref>
</gallery>Early Torajin, who arrived in the [[1st millennium BC|1st millennium BCE]] (encompassing early-[[Jōmon period]] to middle-[[Yayoi period]]), are thought to have introduced rice cultivation and earthenware (such as [[Jōmon pottery]] and [[Yayoi pottery]]) to Japan (mainly in northern Kyushu).

During the formative 5th and 6th centuries, they brought horse breeding and horse driven transportation, stoneware pottery, high temperature iron-working, advanced iron tool manufacturing, and their Chinese-based writing system. In addition to technological and cultural contributions, Toraijin also brought the ideologies of Confucianism and Buddhism from the mainland, which were critical to the state formation and socio-cultural changes during the [[Kofun period]] and [[Asuka period]].
[[File:Koma jinja.jpg|thumb|[[Koma Shrine]], one of the many shrines founded by Toraijin in Japan.]]
The lasting impact of the immigrants from Korea can still be found in placenames within modern Japan in places such as [[Komae, Tokyo#History|Komae (狛江)]] city, deriving from the word "Koma (高麗)" from [[Goguryeo]];<ref>{{cite web |author=Sumiko Enbutsu |author2=Mimi LeBourgeois |date=April 2000 |title=Tokyo Water Walks |url=http://tokyoq.com/the_city/outandabout/out.html |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111005155046/http://tokyoq.com/the_city/outandabout/out.html |archive-date=2011-10-05 |access-date=2008-11-11 |publisher=Tokyo On Foot hosted by Tokyoq |quote=The city name, Komae, probably derived from "Koma," a word referring to Kogyo of ancient Korea, probable origin of the immigrants.}}</ref> [[Niiza, Saitama#History|Niiza (新座)]] city, deriving from the word "Shiragi (新羅)" from [[Silla]];<ref name="Niiza-hp2">{{cite web |title=Niiza city official history |url=https://www.city.niiza.lg.jp/site/bunkazai/bunkazai-niizanoyurai.html |language=ja |location=Japan}}</ref> and possibly [[Nara (city)#Etymology|Nara (奈良)]] city, deriving from the word "Nara (나라)" meaning "country".<ref>{{cite web |author=Ayako Shinomiya Burton |date=November 1994 |title=Japanese Language Planning in Korea 1905-1945 |url=https://summit.sfu.ca/item/6572 |publisher=[[Simon Fraser University]] |pages=11p |quote=particularly around the 5th century, as many Koreans technically skilled in such areas as architecture, ceramics, weaving and iron casting settled in Japan. Korean cultural words such as ''fude'' (writing brush), ''tefu'' (notebook), and even place names such as Koma, Komae and Rebonri, and the most prominent, Nara ("country" in Korea), were introduced into Japan around that time.}}</ref> Many ancient shrines also possess legacy of the immigrants in names such as [[Koma Shrine]] (Goguryeo), {{ill|Shinra Shrine|lt=Shinra Shrine|ja|新羅神社 (多治見市)}} (新羅神社; Silla), and {{ill|Kudara no Ō Shrine|lt=Kudara no Ō Shrine|ja|百済王神社}} (百済王神社; Paekche).

In other instances, Toraijin influence is not deliberately shown within names, but can still be recognized via remnants left by their cultural impact. In many cases, Toraijin elements that have ancient roots in Korea such as [[Korean shamanism]] can be seen throughout modern Japan today. One of the many relics is the presence of ''[[Jangseung]]'', known as ''{{ill|Shōgunhyō|lt=Shōgunhyō|ja|将軍標}}'' (将軍標) in Japan, wooden or stone totems (found normally in pairs) that are believed to ward off evil from sacred places.<ref>{{Cite web |last= |first= |date= |title=장승 |url=http://encykorea.aks.ac.kr/Contents/Index?contents_id=E0048619 |archive-url= |archive-date= |access-date= |website=[[Encyclopedia of Korean Culture]]}}</ref><gallery>
File:Nantes GrandBlottereau jangseungSucheon.jpg|Wooden pair of ''Jaengseungs'' found in Korea.
File:Stone Jangseung in National Folk Museum of Korea - panoramio (2).jpg|Stone pairs found in Korea.
File:Koma-sta.JPG|Wooden pair found in [[Koma Station (Saitama)|Koma station]].
File:Hidaka Saitama Shogunhyo In Koma Shrine 1.JPG|Stone pair found in [[Koma Shrine]].
File:Hidaka Saitama Shodenin Shorakuji Shogunhyo 1.JPG|Stone pair found in {{ill|Shōraku Shrine|lt=Shōraku Shrine|ja|聖天院}} (勝樂寺).
</gallery>Other relics within Japan also point to Toraijin origins such as architectures, artifacts, etc, despite having no direct correlation. The {{ill|Tōkō Temple|lt=Tōkō Temple|ja|東光院 (東京都日の出町)}} (東光院), allegedly founded by the [[Chiba clan]], possesses Korean architecture and elements with many speculating that the temple was originally built by Korean immigrants from Goguryeo or Paekche during the Asuka period.<ref name="お寺">インデックス 編著『訪ねてみたい東京のお寺』インデックス、2006年、324-327p</ref> In fact, every year on May 3, a Korea-themed farming band parades through the area and performs the Korean folk dance (''[[Pungmul]]'').<ref name="民団2">[https://www.mindan.org/old/front/newsDetail9637.html 妙見まつりで韓国伝統公演…百済ゆかりの寺] 在日本大韓民国民団</ref> Another temple, known as the [[Kōryū-ji]], also possesses a wooden statue of Bodhisattva ([[The Buddha|Buddha]]) called the "{{ill|Hōkan Miroku|lt=Hōkan Miroku|ja|弥勒菩薩半跏思惟像}} (宝冠弥勒)", a [[National Treasure (Japan)|national treasure of Japan]] (registered on June 9, 1951); it is believed to have been given from Silla to the [[Hata clan]], the parent clan that built the Kōryū-ji, in the early 7th century.<ref name=":33">{{Citation |chapter=Nihon Shoki |title=Encyclopedic Dictionary of Archaeology |pages=935–936 |year=2021 |chapter-url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1007/978-3-030-58292-0_140217 |access-date= |place=Cham |publisher=Springer International Publishing |doi=10.1007/978-3-030-58292-0_140217 |isbn=978-3-030-58291-3 |chapter-url-access=subscription}}</ref> According to Japanese art historian [[Ōnishi Shunya|Shuya Ōnishi]] (大西 修也), the transmitting of the statue is thought to have been a gift from Silla to its own [[diaspora]]<ref name=":9">{{Cite book |last1=Ōnishi |first1=Shuya |title=Transmitting the forms of divinity: early Buddhist art from Korea and Japan |last2=Washizuka |first2=Hiromitsu |last3=Richard |first3=Naomi Noble |date=2003 |publisher=Japan Society |isbn=978-0-913304-54-9 |location=New York |language=en}}</ref> as Silla produced numerous statues (both wooden and metallic) including the [[Gilt-bronze Maitreya in Meditation (National Treasure No. 83)|Maitreya in Meditation]], a sculpture that is now considered as a sister statue with Japan's Hōkan Miroku, with its signature pose and facial features found only in Silla's craftsmanship.<ref>Pak, Young-Sook and Roderick Whitfield. ''Handbook of Korean Art: Buddhist Sculpture.'' Seoul: Yekyong Publishing, 2002. 108-143.</ref> The possession of the statue became crucial evidence for determining the Hata clan's true origin and approximate period of immigration in modern times. <gallery mode="nolines" perrow="3" heights="150">
File:Hōkan Miroku Statue Colored.png|[[Kōryū-ji#Wooden statue of Bodhisattva|Hōkan Miroku]] ([[Kōryū-ji]])
File:Pensive Bodhisattva 02.jpg|[[Gilt-bronze Maitreya in Meditation (National Treasure No. 83)|Maitreya in Meditation]] ([[Silla]])
</gallery>Other temples such as the [[Hōryū-ji]] is also believed to have take much influence from Toraijin after the original building (built in 607) was burnt down and was reconstructed in 670.<ref>{{cite book |last=光谷 |first=拓実 |author-link= |url=https://repository.nabunken.go.jp/dspace/bitstream/11177/309/1/BA67898227_2001_032_033.pdf |title=法隆寺五重塔心柱の年輪年代 |year=2001 |language=ja}}</ref> The temple is thought to have been built by Toraijin from Paekche<ref name="Gupta2008">{{cite book |author=Sameer Das Gupta |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=H4ckAQAAIAAJ&q=H%C5%8Dryu-ji+baekje |title=Advanced history of Buddhism: monasteries and temples |date=January 1, 2008 |publisher=Cyber Tech Publications |isbn=9788178843438 |pages=289–}}</ref> who brought the temple's sacred artifact and another national treasure of Japan (registered on June 9, 1951), the {{ill|Kudara Kanon|lt=Kudara Kanon|ja|百済観音}} (百済観音; {{Literal translation|Avalokiteśvara of Paekche}})<ref>{{Cite book |last=小泉 |first=惠英 |title=特別展百済観音 |publisher=執筆は田中義恭 |year=1988 |pages=148 |language=ja}}</ref> similar to the Hōkan Miroku of the Kōryū-ji. In January 2026, the Hōryū-ji temple was chosen as the place to tour during Korea's President [[Lee Jae Myung]]'s visit with Japan's Prime Minister [[Sanae Takaichi]] as Lee wished to visit Takaicihi's hometown of [[Nara Prefecture|Nara]] (where the temple is also located), and because the temple's architecture was influenced by Korean culture, signifying the two countries' historical connections.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2026-01-09 |title=日韓首脳がそろって法隆寺へ…13・14日に高市首相の地元・奈良に滞在 建築様式が朝鮮半島文化の影響 |trans-title=The leaders of Japan and South Korea plan to visit Horyuji Temple together. On the 13th and 14th, they will stay in Prime Minister Takaichi's hometown of Nara. The architectural style is influenced by Korean culture. |url=https://www.fnn.jp/articles/-/985107 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260110013429/https://www.fnn.jp/articles/985107 |archive-date=2026-01-10 |access-date= |website=FNNプライムオンライン}}</ref><gallery mode="nolines" perrow="3" heights="150">
File:Kudara Kannon. British Museum.jpg|{{ill|Kudara Kanon|lt=Kudara Kanon|ja|百済観音}} ([[Hōryū-ji]])
</gallery>As such, it is evident that influence from Toraijin is both direct and inert depending on the detail, with some possessing elements such as names that directly allude to Toraijin roots (i.e. Koma for Goguryeo) or having innuendos such as architecture, artifacts, and practices that provide an insight to their likely Toraijin origins.

According to modern Japanese academia, in each major epoch in Japanese history, Toraijin arriving from the Korean peninsula acted as transmitters and transplanters of advanced continental technology and culture to the Japanese archipelago; just as the population groups on the Korean peninsula experienced similar transformations with the arrival of millet and rice agriculture, bronze and iron objects and technologies, and culture and religion from further west and north in the continent.<ref name=":3" />

== History ==
The periods of arrival of the Toraijin can be divided into four categories: 2nd–3rd century BCE, around 5th century BCE ([[Five kings of Wa]]'s reign), late 5th–6th century, and 7th century.<ref name=":0" />

=== Early periods ===
The early Toraijin, known as the indigenous [[Jōmon people]], were engaged in subsistence based primarily on fishing, hunting, and gathering. Early to middle [[Jōmon period]] pottery, known as {{ill|Sobatashikidoki|lt=Sobatashikidoki|ja|曽畑式土器}} (曽畑式土器), show significant similarity with the [[Jeulmun pottery period|Jeulmun period]] pottery of Korea not only in the surface patterns, but also in the use of [[talc]] mixed into the clay, giving it the signature brownish color.<ref name=":6">{{Cite journal |last=Nonno |first=Tresi |title=A preliminary attempt to compare ornaments of Jeulmun and Jōmon |url=https://www.academia.edu/44113048 |year=2020 |journal=Cultural Anthropology and Ethnosemiotics |volume=6 |issue=2 |pages=30–41}}</ref> Both styles are part of the bigger [[Comb Ceramic|Comb Ceramic pottery]] which is found worldwide ([[Xinglongwa culture]] in [[Northeast China]]; [[Comb Ceramic culture]] in [[Northern Europe|Northeast Europe]], etc), however, early Jeulmun and Jōmon styles and their production methods are unique to Korea and Japan.<ref name=":6" /> Despite starting similar, Korea's Jeulmun period is believed to have ended much earlier than Japan's Jōmon period (around 500 years) due to the incoming migrants.<gallery>
File:KoreanEarthenwareJar4000BCEAmsa-DongNearSeoul.jpg|[[Jeulmun pottery period|Jeulmun period]] (c. 8000–1500 BCE) pottery
File:Middle Jomon Period rope pottery 5000-4000BC.jpg|[[Jōmon period]] (c. 8000–300 BCE) pottery
</gallery>After the Jōmon period, a new batch of immigrants arrived in Japan at a time known as the [[Yayoi period]] who introduced wet-rice farming to the archipelago. Similar to the Jeulmun–Jōmon style pottery, Yayoi pottery is often associated with the [[Mumun pottery period|Mumun period]] pottery of Korea due to the lack of decorations found in the design and for its signature "plain ({{Korean|hangul=무문|hanja=無文|rr=Mumun|lit=No decoration}})" look.<ref name="Bale2001">{{cite journal |last=Bale |first=Martin T. |year=2001 |title=Archaeology of Early Agriculture in Korea: An Update on Recent Developments |journal=Bulletin of the Indo-Pacific Prehistory Association |volume=21 |issue=5 |pages=77–84}}</ref> The Mumun people are believed to have replaced the Jeulmun people around 1500 BCE who then migrated to the archipelago which marked the beginning of the Yayoi period of Japan. Similar to the Mumun period being labelled as the "Korean [[Bronze Age]]",<ref name="Kim1996">{{cite book |last=Kim |first=Seung Og |title=Political Competition and Social Transformation: The Development of Residence, Residential Ward, and Community in Prehistoric Taegongni of Southwestern Korea |publisher=University of Michigan Press |year=1996 |location=Ann Arbor}}</ref> middle-Yayoi period Toraijin arrived with bronze technology.<ref>[[Richard J. Pearson|Pearson, Richard J.]] Chiefly Exchange Between Kyushu and Okinawa, Japan, in the Yayoi Period. ''Antiquity'' 64(245) 912–22, 1990.</ref><gallery>
File:Korea-Bronze.age-Jinju-Pot-01.jpg|[[Mumun pottery period|Mumun period]] (c. 1500–300 BCE) pottery
File:壺形土器（弥生土器）恵山式.jpg|[[Yayoi period]] (c. 1000 BCE–300 CE) pottery
</gallery>The direct descendants of these two groups are believed to have resulted in the [[Samhan people]],<ref name=":15">{{Cite book |last=Mizoguchi|first=Kōji|title=The archaeology of Japan: from the earliest rice farming villages to the rise of the state|date=2013|publisher=Cambridge University Press|isbn=978-0-521-88490-7|series=Cambridge world archaeology|location=Cambridge|pages=53}}</ref><ref name=":22">{{Cite journal |last=Miyamoto|first=Kazuo|year=2016|title=Archaeological Explanation for the Diffusion Theory of the Japonic and Koreanic Language|url=https://catalog.lib.kyushu-u.ac.jp/opac_download_md/1812319/JJA4-1.pdf|journal=Japanese Journal of Archeology|volume=4|pages=53–75}}</ref> an ancient group that possessed many similarities with the contemporary ancient Japanese of [[Wakoku|Wa]]. However, due to the constant migration from the north by the [[Yemaek|Yemaek people]], the indigenous Samhan people eventually assimilated with the incoming Yemaek people and became what are known as the [[Three Kingdoms of Korea|Three Kingdoms period]] Koreans.<ref name=":04">{{Citation |last=Vovin|first=Alexander|chapter=Origins of the Japanese Language|date=2017-09-26|title=Oxford Research Encyclopedia of Linguistics|chapter-url=https://oxfordre.com/linguistics/view/10.1093/acrefore/9780199384655.001.0001/acrefore-9780199384655-e-277|access-date=2026-05-24|publisher=Oxford University Press|language=en|doi=10.1093/acrefore/9780199384655.013.277|isbn=978-0-19-938465-5|chapter-url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref name=":72">{{Cite journal |last1=Wang|first1=Rui|last2=Wang|first2=Chuan-Chao|date=2022-08-08|title=Human genetics: The dual origin of Three Kingdoms period Koreans|journal=Current Biology|volume=32|issue=15|pages=R844–R847|bibcode=2022CBio...32.R844W|doi=10.1016/j.cub.2022.06.044|issn=0960-9822|pmid=35944486|doi-access=free}}</ref>

=== Kofun period ===
[[File:5th_century_Korea.png|thumb|Korea in the mid-late [[5th century]], middle of the [[Kofun period]]. Multiple waves of migration to Japan happened due to constant wars and political unrest.|368x368px]]
During the [[Kofun period]] and the turbulent [[Three Kingdoms period of Korea]], there were extensive migrations from Korean polities to the Japanese archipelago, particularly from [[Paekche]] and [[Gaya confederacy|Kaya confederacy]], both of which developed friendship as well as economic and military alliances with [[Yamato Kingship]]. According to the ''[[Nihon Shoki]]'' and ''[[Kojiki]]'', the first major arrival to Japan was during the reign of [[Emperor Ōjin]]. Due to a major upheaval on the Korean peninsula at that time, it is believed that many people from the peninsula migrated to Japan to escape the political chaos and subsequently introduced new technology such iron tools, irrigation technology, Chinese knowledge, religions and much more. The tools and technology they brought with them may have revolutionized the production methods and labor patterns that had existed until then. These immigrants from Korea also introduced [[horse]]s, a foreign species to the archipelago at the time, and [[horse harness]]es.<ref name=":5">{{Cite web |title=Horses in Japan |url=https://www.japan-experience.com/prepare-trip/know/understand-japan/horse-japanese-culture |access-date= |website=www.japan-experience.com |language=en |publication-date=2024-02-27}}</ref> With this, horse riding became a common practice in Japan and were later incorporated into future military purposes.<ref name=":5" />

Minimal travel occurred between the kingdom of Silla and the archipelago owing to a hostile relationship between the Yamato Kingship and Silla, especially after the [[Silla–Goguryeo and Paekche–Kaya–Wa War]]. The Wa elites, such as Yamato elites in Kinki, Tsukushi elites in Fukuoka, and Kibi elites in Okayama, sought to establish socio-political advantages in the archipelago and welcomed and integrated the newcomers with peninsular goods and advanced technology.<ref name=":3" /> In 552&nbsp;CE, King [[Seong of Baekje]] sent envoys to the Yamato court, bringing Buddha statues and Buddhist classics, and Buddhist culture was also introduced to Japan. After Buddhism was introduced to Japan, it became one of the main religions in Japan and a part of today's Japanese culture.

These immigrants settled and re-established themselves as farmers, iron technicians, horse breeders, merchants and traders, dam builders, craftsmen, among others, earning them the name "Imaki no Tehito (今來才技, “recently arrived skilled artisans”)" in the ''[[Nihon Shoki]]''.<ref name=":3" /> Groups arriving from the peninsula have settled in and formed communities in various parts of the archipelago, including Fukuoka in northern Kyushu to Okayama on the Inland Sea, to the Kyoto–Osaka– Nara area, to Gunma north of Tokyo, and as far as Sendai in northeastern Honshu. Once fully settled on the Japanese Archipelago, these immigrants became known as "Kikajin", or "naturalized immigrants".<ref name=":3" /> While migrants initially settled in Kyushu due to geographic proximity to the peninsula, by the fourth century, migrants had shifted their destination to the Kinki region, the core base of the Yamato elites, of Nara, Osaka, Kyoto, and Otsu region.
[[File:Haniwa Terracotta Figurine (30062123075).jpg|thumb|285x285px|''[[Haniwa]]'' depicting a Toraijin from [[Kaya confederacy]] during the Kofun period.<ref name=":4">{{Cite web |title=九州国立博物館 - 特別展：「加耶」 |url=https://www.kyuhaku.jp/exhibition/exhibition_s67.html |access-date= |website=九州国立博物館 |language=ja}}</ref> It is described to be depicting an immigrant due to the long sleeves that were worn by Toraijin at the time.<ref name=":4" /><ref name=":2">{{Cite book |last=Torii |first=Ryūzō |title=有史以前の日本 |year=1925 |pages=621–622 |language=ja |trans-title=Japan before History}}</ref>]]
Anthropologist [[Torii Ryūzō]] also recounted the attires worn by Toraijin during Kofun period stating "[the Kofun period Toraijin had unique] customs, including love of swords, skills in bow and arrows, tied hair, beads decorations, long sleeves and baggy pants, leather boots, and daggers on the belt, are exactly what you can find in early northeast Asia. The same can be said about their arrows with feathers and whistling arrowheads."<ref name=":2" /> Torii labeled the previous Yayoi group as the "earthly tribe ''[kunitsu kami; 国津神]''" of Japan while labeling the newly introduced Kofun group as the "heavenly tribe ''[amatsu kami; 天津神]''". This sentiment was carried over by a fellow anthropologist, {{ill|喜田貞吉|lt=Sadakichi Kita|ja|}} (喜田 貞吉) who associated the "heavenly tribe (Kofun people)" of Japan to the [[Buyeo]] people stating that "[...] the incoming heavenly tribe, who conquered, appeased, annexed, and assimilated the [[Yayoi people|existing population]] and constituted the [[Yamato people|grand Japanese]], were previously residents of [[Buyeo|a region in the continent]]. [The Buyeo people] had moved to the Japanese islands at some point."<ref>{{Cite book |last=Kita |first=Sadakichi |title=喜田貞吉著作集 |publisher=[[Heibonsha]] |year=1979 |edition=8 |pages=375–379 |language=ja |trans-title=Works of Sadakichi Kita}}</ref>

20th century linguist, {{ill|金沢庄三郎|lt=Shōzaburo Kanazawa|ja|}} (金沢 庄三郎) even wrote that "the [[Korean language]] belongs to the same line of languages as our [[Japonic languages|[Japanese] language]]. This is a branch of our language, just as the [[Ryukyuan languages|Ryukyu dialect]] is" in his book {{Nihongo|2=日韓両国語同系論|3=Nikkan ryōkokugo dōkeiron}} in 1910,<ref>{{Cite book |last=Kanazawa |first=Shōzaburo |title=日韓両国語同系論 |publisher=[[Sanseidō]] |year=1910 |pages=7 |language=ja |trans-title=Theory on Japanese‑Korean languages Common Language Family}}</ref> postulating that the "''Theory on Japanese‑Korean Common Ancestry"'', also known as ''[[Nissen dōsoron]]'', that was introduced during the [[Korea under Japanese rule|Japanese annexation period of Korea]] was factually correct. Kanazawa essentially categorized the Buyeo people, who were Koreanic speaking [[Yemaek|Yemaek people]], and Kofun period Toraijin as the same ethnic group, predicating that because the Kofun people were a key component of Japanese history, genealogy and therefore identity, the Buyeo people and their language were also inherently Japanese.<ref group="Notes">However, due to the popular belief that Japan was more sophisticated than Korea at the time, Japanese scholars purposefully evaded claiming that Korea was the main pillar of both groups, but rather, it was propagandized to claim that Korea was the offshoot branch of the bigger Japan-Korea ethnicity. Hence, why Koreans were regarded as being "part" of the Japanese race, and not vice versa.</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Allen |first=Chizuko |title=Early Migrations, Conquests, and Common Ancestry: Theorizing Japanese Origins in Relation with Korea |publisher=Sungkyun Journal of East Asian Studies |year=2008 |volume=8 |pages=105–130 |language=en}}</ref> Regardless of the macro-ethnocentric position taken by [[Empire of Japan|Imperial Japan]] in regards to Korea at the time, a similar conclusion was drawn over a century later in 2022<ref name=":02">{{Cite journal |last=Miyamoto |first=Kazuo |date=6 January 2022 |title=The emergence of 'Transeurasian' language families in Northeast Asia as viewed from archaeological evidence |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/357634119 |journal=ResearchGate |pages=}}</ref> supporting that even linguistically, Japonic and Koreanic speakers were indeed heavily related.

[[National Museum of Nature and Science]] held a special exhibition in May 2025 that revolved around the genetic makeup of the Japanese surrounding specific periods.<ref name="JP">{{Cite AV media |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WqaYQRBQ__Q |title=日本人の起源を探る！特別展「古代ＤＮＡ―日本人のきた道―」 |date=5 May 2025 |last=【国立科学博物館公式】かはくチャンネル |language=ja |access-date= |via=YouTube}}</ref> The director of the museum stated that the majority of the relics found during the Kofun period bore heavy resemblance with those found in Korea. He also emphasized that the immigrants who brought new technology entered after the late-Yayoi period and are considered as main contributors to the modern Japanese people's genetic makeup.<ref name="JP" /><gallery mode="nolines" perrow="6">

</gallery>These new waves of immigrants from Korea continued well into the Asuka period. However, their influence is believed to have reached its peak during the Kofun period and slowly fell off afterward with numbers dwindling over time. Since then, Japan and its demographics began to homogenize from that point on.

=== Asuka period ===
After entering the [[Asuka period]], many Japanese royals and ministers believed in Buddhism, such as [[Prince Shōtoku]] and Soga Mako, and devoted themselves to promoting Buddhism. The reason why [[Paekche]] people went to Japan was that Japan asked Paekche for craftsmen and {{ill|Doctor of the five classics|lt=doctors of the Five Classics|ja|五経博士}} and escaped from [[Goguryeo]].<ref>森公章「『帰化人と古代国家を読む』、平野前掲書解説</ref>

In the 7th century, exiles from [[Paekche]], which had been defeated at the [[Battle of Baekgang]], entered Japan. The technology and culture brought by the Toraijin contributed to the advanced development of Japan at that time.<ref name=":0" /><ref>平野邦雄『帰化人と古代国家』吉川弘文館、2007年、p.2</ref> Toraijin occupied an important position in the military and political affairs of the Yamato regime due to their advanced skills in arms manufacturing, weaving, and agriculture. They also made significant contributions to the development of Japanese culture.<ref name=":1" />

{{Main|Asadal}}
[[File:Excerpt_of_Yegun's_Epitaph.png|right|frameless]]
{{Blockquote|text=『日本餘噍 據扶桑以逋誅』
----
"The refugees of Ilbon (日本; referring to [[Paekche]]) safely retreated with the help of [[Yamato Kingship|Busang Kingdom]] (扶桑; referring to Japan) from the invaders ([[Silla]]–[[Tang dynasty|Tang]] alliance)."|author=|source=678 CE|title=''Excerpt from "Yegun's Epithaph"''}}It is believed that the Toraijin refugees from Paekche also brought nationalistic ideology as well.

Historically, up until the [[Yamato Kingship|Yamato Kingdom]] changed its name from "[[Wakoku]] (倭国)" then "[[Yamato Kingship|Yamato]] (ヤマト)" to "Nihon (日本)", [[Baekje|Paekche]] had used the same characters "Ilbon (日本)", literally meaning "Land where the sun rises" (no relations to [[Japan]]) when it colloquially addressed itself (as seen in {{ill|Yegun|lt=Yegun|ko|예군}}, a Paekche nationalist and loyalist of [[Uija of Baekje|King Uija]], in his epitaph),<ref name=":7">{{Cite book |last=王 |first=連龍 |title=百濟人祢軍墓誌考論 |publisher=社會科學戰線 |year=2011 |edition=第7期 (總第193期) |pages=123–129 |language=zh}}</ref><ref name=":8">{{Cite book |last=東野 |first=治之 |title=百済人祢軍墓誌の「日本」 |publisher=岩波書店 |year=2012 |pages=2–4 |language=ja}}</ref> seeming to have carried over the meaning of "Morning Land" from [[Asadal]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=금석문·문자자료 < 한국 고대 사료 DB |url=https://db.history.go.kr/ancient/level.do?levelId=gskh_002_0030_0040_0030 |access-date= |website=db.history.go.kr}}</ref> Believed to have been created around 678 CE, the epitaph is the oldest account in East Asian history to have used the term "Land where the sun rises (日本)" (Wang 2011; Tono 2012).<ref name=":7" /><ref name=":8" />

== Notable Toraijin clans ==
{{Further|Japanese clans#Immigrant clans}}

The Yamato basin was the home of powerful clans with Toraijin connections, such as the [[Soga clan]] with [[Paekche]] affiliation and which emerged as the most powerful clan in the Yamato by the middle of 6th century, and the [[Yamato no Aya clan]] with roots in the [[Kaya confederacy]] and [[Paekche]].
[[File:Jingū Kōgō.jpg|thumb|260x260px|[[Empress Jingū]] was of [[Silla]] descent through [[Amenohiboko]] ([[Tajima clan]]).]]
[[File:Emperor Kammu large.jpg|thumb|262x262px|[[Emperor Kanmu]] was of [[Paekche]] descent through [[Takano no Niigasa]] ([[Yamato no Fuhito clan]]).]]
Influential Toraijin clans with imperial ties included the [[Tajima clan]] (多遅摩氏) of Silla descent, as well as [[Kudara no Konikishi clan]] and [[Yamato no Fuhito clan]], both of Paekche descent. During the 3rd or 4th century, [[Amenohiboko]], a prince from [[Silla]] and also a Toraijin, immigrated to Japan and became the ancestor to [[Empress Jingū]] while founding the Tajima clan. Early in the eighth century, Lady [[Takano no Niigasa]], a member of the Yamato no Fuhito clan and a descendant of [[Muryeong of Baekje|Muryeong of]] [[Seong of Baekje|Baekje]], married Prince Shirakabe (the future [[Emperor Kōnin]]) and gave birth to Yamanobe in 737 in Nara, who was enthroned in 781 and became [[Emperor Kanmu]].<ref name=":3" />

Families such as the [[Tatara clan (Japan)|Tatara clan]] became the parent house of powerful clans such as the [[Ōuchi clan]].

Other representative Toraijin groups of the 4th and 5th centuries were the [[Hata clan]], and the [[Kawachinofumi clan]] (西文氏). These Toraijin possessed superior technology and ability, and were fundamental to Japan's nation-building. The Hata clan is descended from [[Yuzuki no Kimi]], who came from Silla on the Korean Peninsula around the 4th or 5th century. Yuzuki no Kimi came to Kyushu with 30,000 to 40,000 laborers from 127 prefectures. They served the Yamato royal court as officials in charge of finances. His headquarters was originally located in Yamaboshi, Kyoto, but he later moved to Uzumasa (Kyoto City). Along with their activities in the center of Japan, the descendants of the Hata extended their influence nationwide, from Owari and Mino to Bicchu and Chiku.<ref name=":0" />

* [[Aya clan]] (Paekche/Kaya)
* [[Hata clan]] (Silla)
* [[Koma clan]] (Goguryeo)
* [[Kudara no Konikishi clan]] (Paekche)
* [[Ōtomo clan (immigrant)|Ōtomo clan]] (Silla)
* [[Ōuchi clan]] (Paekche/Kaya)
* [[Tatara clan (Japan)|Tatara clan]] (Kaya)
* [[Toyoda clan]] (Paekche)
* [[Yamato no Fuhito clan]] (Paekche)

{{Further|List of Toraijin people}}
[[File:Yuzuki no Kimi.jpg|thumb|301x301px|[[Yuzuki no Kimi]] of [[Paekche]].]]

* [[Amenohiboko]] – Founder of the [[Tajima clan]]. Ancestor of god of sweets, [[Tajimamori]] and [[Empress Jingū]].

* [[Prince Junda]] – Founder of the [[Yamato no Fuhito clan]].

Suspected individuals:

* [[Fujiwara no Kamatari]](?) – Founder of the [[Fujiwara clan]]. Suspected to be a Toraijin and may even be [[Buyeo Pung]].
* [[Takenouchi no Sukune]](?) – Father to founders of Toraijin clans such as [[Hata no Yashiro]] ([[Hata clan]]) and [[Soga no Ishikawa]] ([[Soga clan]]). Descendants include "[[Soga no Karako]] (蘇我韓子)", meaning "Korean person of Soga" and his son, [[Soga no Koma]], meaning "[[Goguryeo]] person of Soga" of the Soga clan. Suspected to be a Toraijin.

== Toraijin gods ==
Many deities, known as ''[[kami]]'' in Japan, are believed to have been introduced by Toraijin as well.

=== Shinra Myōjin ===
{{Main|Shinra Myōjin|Ōtomo clan (immigrant)}}

[[File:Statue_of_shinra_myojin,_Mii-dera.jpg|thumb|226x226px|A statue of [[Shinra Myōjin]], the ''[[kami]]'' from [[Silla]].]]
It is said that the history of the [[Ōtomo clan (immigrant)|Ōtomo clan]], a clan from [[Silla]], was heavily intertwined with [[Shinra Myōjin]] ({{literal translation|''Shining deity of Silla''}}), a [[Buddhist god]] associated with the [[Jimon and Sanmon|Jimon]] branch of [[Tendai]], a school of [[Japanese Buddhism]]. His name is derived from the name of a historical Korean kingdom, Silla.

Professor [[Sujung Kim]] (김수정) at [[DePauw University]] of [[religious studies]] who specializes in history of [[Buddhism]] in East Asia, claims that the Ōtomo clan's special ties to deities such as the Shinra Myōjin may provide an insight to the clan's possible origins.<ref name=":32">{{Cite book |last=Kim |first=Sunjung |title=Shinra Myōjin and Buddhist networks of the East Asian "Mediterranean" |publisher=University of Hawaii Press |year=2019 |isbn=978-0824888442 |language=en}}</ref>

It is said that the Ōtomo clan was one of the earliest clans to commemorate Shinra Myōjin and was involved in promoting the veneration of said deity. Kim posited that the Shinra Myōjin originally being a Silla god sheds light on the possibility of the clan being Silla immigrants<ref name=":32" /> as it was common for immigrants from specific regions to be left with commemorating gods from the same origins as seen with the Hata clan and the ''kami'' Inari.

=== Inari ===
{{Main|Inari Ōkami|Hata clan|Cheonggu#Possible connections to Japan}}

[[File:A_man_confronted_with_an_apparition_of_the_Fox_goddess.jpg|thumb|256x256px|[[Inari Ōkami|Inari]] appearing in front of a warrior.]]
Additional evidence alludes to the foreign origins of the ''[[kami]]'' [[Inari Ōkami|Inari]], a deity that looks over [[Red fox|foxes]], [[Fertility (soil)|fertility]], [[rice]], [[tea]] and [[sake]], of [[agriculture]] and [[Industrial sector|industry]], of general prosperity and worldly success.

[[Fushimi Inari-taisha]], the same shrine built by the [[Hata clan]] and one of the most influential shrines to officially celebrate the god Inari, stated that the fox deity was most likely not of Japanese origin and had most likely arrived in Japan from the kingdoms of the Korean peninsula.<ref name=":13">{{Cite web |title=「おいなりさん物語」 ~伏見稲荷大社~ |url=https://inari.jp/about/story/ |website=Fushimi Inari Taisha |language=Japanese}}</ref> It states that during the [[Three Kingdoms of Korea]] period, foxes were widely celebrated as gods and were deified as protectors of agriculture and prosperity due to the influence of [[Buddhism]].

This concept of an agricultural deity was later carried over to the Japanese archipelago by other immigrant clans which arrived in Japan in the earlier centuries<ref name="Higo">Higo, Kazuo.  "Inari Shinkō no Hajime".  ''Inari Shinkō'' (ed. Hiroji Naoe).  Tokyo: Yūzankaku Shuppan, 1983.</ref> and was given the name "稲荷 (いなり)" in ''[[kanji]]'' which means "carrying rice", (literally "rice load") first found in the ''[[Ruijū Kokushi]]'' in 892 AD.

Scholars such as {{ill|Kazuo Higo|ja|肥後和男}} (肥後 和男) suggest that the Hata clan began the formal worship of Inari as an agriculture ''kami'' in the late 5th century<ref name="Higo" /> as the name "Inari" does not appear in classical [[Japanese mythology]]<ref name="McMullin 1988. pp. 266-267">McMullin (1988). pp. 266-267.</ref> which most likely indicates that the god is foreign.

=== Susanoo-no-Mikoto ===
{{Main|Susanoo-no-Mikoto|Gozu Tennō}}

[[File:11.36845-Utagawa Kuniteru I-Museum of Fine Art Boston.jpg|thumb|248x248px|[[Susanoo-no-Mikoto|Susanoo]] kills the Yamata no Orochi. ([[Kuniteru|Utagawa Kuniteru]])]]
There may be some connections to other foreign deities especially with the most commonly mentioned [[Susanoo-no-Mikoto]], brother of ''kami'' [[Amaterasu]].

A few myths, such as that of Susanoo's descent in Soshimori in Silla, seem to suggest a connection between the god and the [[Korea|Korean peninsula]]. Indeed, some scholars have hypothesized that the deities who were eventually conflated with Susanoo, Mutō Tenjin, and Gozu Tennō, may have had Korean origins as well, with the name "Mutō" (武塔, [[Historical kana orthography|historical orthography]]: ''mutau'') being linked with the Korean word ''[[Korean shamanism|mudang]]'' "shamaness," and "Gozu" being explained as a [[calque]] of "Soshimori", here interpreted as being derived from a Korean toponym meaning "Bull's (''[[wiktionary:소#Etymology_1|so]]'') Head (''[[wiktionary:마리#Middle_Korean|mari]]'')".<ref name="McMullin 1988. pp. 266-267"/> For further information, see [[Hata clan#Title - Uzumasa|etymology of the ''title'' "Uzumasa"]]. The name "Susanoo" itself has been interpreted as being related to the [[Middle Korean]] title ''[[wiktionary:스승|susung]]'' ([[Idu script|transliterated]] as 次次雄 or 慈充), meaning "master" or "shaman", notably applied to [[Namhae of Silla|Namhae]], the second king of Silla, in the ''[[Samguk sagi|Samguk]]'' ''[[Samguk sagi|sagi]]''.<ref name="HistKor">{{cite book |last1=Lee |first1=Ki-Moon |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=2AmspKX3beoC&pg=PA75 |title=A History of the Korean Language |last2=Ramsey |first2=S. Robert |publisher=Cambridge University Press |year=2011 |isbn=978-1-139-49448-9 |page=75}}</ref> Susanoo is thus supposed in this view to have originally been a foreign god (蕃神, ''banshin''), perhaps a deified shaman, whose origins may be traced back to Korea.<ref>Gadeleva (2000). p. 168.</ref><!--Editor's note: The paragraph above was taken from the Susanoo-no-Mikoto article.-->

The theories surrounding Susanoo being introduced to Japan as a foreign god coincide with other ''kami'' such as Inari, and may have been introduced in a similar fashion. Their Silla roots (Inari–Hata; Shinra Myōjin–Ōtomo; Susanoo/Gozu Tennō–Soshimori) may indicate that the ''kami'' were originally from the peninsula until they were brought over to Japan by Korean immigrants. Ironically, the origins of ''kami'' such as Susanoo was retrospectively used as a tool to justify the [[Korea under Japanese rule|Japanese annexation of Korea]] and the [[Nissen dōsoron|assimilation of its people]], claiming that Susanoo was a native Japanese god that first arrived and founded Silla, rather than a Silla-originating god that moved to Japan. Elder [[Shinto]] priest, [[Tsunoda Tadayuki]] postulated that Susanoo was in fact analogous with [[Tan'gun]], a native Korean deity<ref>{{Blockquote|text="Tsunoda identified Dangun with Susano-o-no-mikoto 素戔嗚尊 (a younger brother of Amaterasu in Japanese myths) in light of the supposed mythological relations between Korea and Japan in antiquity. This was also a compromise between the Hirata school’s ethnocentric Shinto ideal—“Japan as the origin of the world”—and the latest theory concerning “the identical origins of Japanese and Koreans” advocated by some historians and anthropologists. Further, Tsunoda’s interest in Dangun coincided with the emergence of a Korean nationalism focused on this deity. Thus the Shintoists’ petition reverberated beyond their original intent; when the Japanese government faced the March First Independent Movement of 1919 in Korea, Tsunoda’s opinion concerning Dangun was quoted by a group of liberal Diet members to accuse the colonial government of misrule. Then, around the time of the inauguration ceremony of the Chōsen Shrine on 15 October 1925, several Shinto activists, including leading figures in the priesthood, petitioned the Governor-General to enshrine Dangun in it."|author=''Suga Kōji''|title=''A Concept of “Overseas Shinto Shrines” - A Pantheistic Attempt by Ogasawara Shōzō and Its Limitations''}}</ref><ref name=":022">{{Cite journal |last1=Kōji |first1=Suga |date=2010 |title=A Concept of "Overseas Shinto Shrines": A Pantheistic Attempt by Ogasawara Shōzō and Its Limitations |url=https://nirc.nanzan-u.ac.jp/journal/6/issue/180/article/1292 |journal=[[Japanese Journal of Religious Studies]] |volume=37 |issue=1 |pages=47–74 |issn=0304-1042 |jstor=27822899}}</ref> and advocated the amalgamation of the Japanese ''kami'' with the Korean god. A similar phenomenon happened prior with Susanoo and [[Gozu Tennō]], another foreign god that may have Korean origin.<ref name="McMullin2">{{cite journal |last1=McMullin |first1=Neil |date=February 1988 |title=On Placating the Gods and Pacifying the Populace: The Case of the Gion "Goryō" Cult |journal=History of Religions |publisher=The University of Chicago Press |volume=27 |issue=3 |pages=270–293 |doi=10.1086/463123 |jstor=1062279 |s2cid=162357693}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Gozu Tennou 牛頭天王 |url=http://www.aisf.or.jp/~jaanus/deta/g/gozutennou.htm |access-date=2020-03-31 |website=Japanese Architecture and Art Net Users System (JAANUS)}}</ref>

=== Others ===
Other kami of speculated foreign origins include:

* [[Gozu Tennō]] – A ''kami'' that is often amalgamated with the aforementioned Susanoo.<ref name="Torrance 2019 277–318">{{Cite journal |last=Torrance |first=Richard |date=2019 |title=Ōnamochi: The Great God who Created All Under Heaven |journal=Japanese Journal of Religious Studies |volume=46 |issue=2 |pages=277–318 |doi=10.18874/jjrs.46.2.2019.277-317 |issn=0304-1042 |jstor=26854516 |s2cid=209442321 |doi-access=free}}</ref><ref name="McMullin2"/>
* [[Ōkuninushi]] – The son (or descendant) of Susanoo who is also often associated with Korea due to his father.<ref name="Torrance 2019 277–318"/>
* [[Kawa-no-Kami]] – Also known as "Kahaku (河伯)". May have been influenced by China's [[Hebo]]<ref name=":14">{{Cite web |title=Encyclopedia of Shinto詳細 |url=https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/?id=9377 |access-date=2021-09-04 |website=國學院大學デジタルミュージアム |language=ja}}</ref> and Korea's [[Habaek]].<ref name="Torrance 2019 277–318"/>

== Population estimates ==

The method proposed by Koyama (1978)<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Koyama |first=Shuzo |date=1978 |title=Jomon Subsistence and Population |url=https://minpaku.repo.nii.ac.jp/record/3481/files/SES02_002.pdf |journal=Senri Ethnological Studies |language=en |volume=2 |issue= |pages=1–65 |doi= |issn= |jstor= |id= |authorlink= |accessdate=}}</ref> to calculate the ratio of the number of sites from multiple periods enables population estimates for the Jomon and Yayoi periods, which in turn enables the demographic simulations of Koyama and Sugitoh (1984)<ref>{{Cite journal |author=小山修三 |author2=杉藤重信 |date=1984 |title=縄文人口シミュレーション |url=https://minpaku.repo.nii.ac.jp/record/4444/files/KH_009_1_001.pdf |journal=国立民族学博物館研究報告 |language=ja |volume=9 |issue=1 |pages=1–39 |doi= |issn= |jstor= |id= |accessdate=}}</ref> and Hanihara (1987)<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Hanihara |first=Kazuo |date=1987 |title=Estimation of the Number of Early Migrants to Japan: A Simulative Study |url= |journal=Journal of the Anthropological Society of Nippon |language=en |volume=95 |issue=3 |pages=391–403 |doi= 10.1537/ase1911.95.391|issn= |jstor= |id= |authorlink= |accessdate=|doi-access=free }}</ref> into the prehistoric period of Japan.

The current consensus in regards to Toraijin population estimation is highly debated.

Hanihara argued that more than 3 million (3025 people/year) immigrated to the Japanese archipelago between 300 BCE&nbsp;– 700&nbsp;CE. In addition, based on estimates from studies of Senzuka (cemeteries of “thousand tombs”) belonging to the Toraijin from the southwestern Korean peninsula and their descendants, Shinichirō Ishiwatari postulated that at least a million people from the peninsula arrived in the archipelago just during the 125 years between 475–600 CE.<ref name=":3" />

However, the hypothesis of a very large number of migrants coming to the Japanese archipelago, as represented by Hanihara and Ishiwatari, was criticized by later simulation studies (Nakahashi and Iizuka 1998,<ref>{{Cite journal |author=中橋孝博 |author2=飯塚勝 |date=1998 |title=北部九州の縄文～弥生移行期に関する人類学的考察 |url=https://www.jstage.jst.go.jp/article/asj1998/106/1/106_1_31/_article/-char/ja/ |journal=人類学雑誌 |language=ja |volume=106 |issue=1 |pages=31–53 |doi=10.1537/asj1998.106.31 |issn= |jstor= |id= |accessdate=|doi-access=free }}</ref> 2008<ref>{{Cite journal |author=中橋孝博 |author2=飯塚勝 |date=2008 |title=北部九州の縄文～弥生移行期に関する人類学的考察（2） |url=https://www.jstage.jst.go.jp/article/asj/116/2/116_2_131/_article/-char/ja/ |journal=人類学雑誌 |language=ja |volume=116 |issue=2 |pages=131–143 |doi=10.1537/asj.116.131 |issn= |jstor= |id= |accessdate=|doi-access=free }}</ref>) with Aoki and Tuljapurkar (2000)<ref>{{Cite journal |author=Aoki, K. |author2=Tuljapurkar, S. |date=2000 |title=Hanihara's Conundrum Revisited: Theoretical Estimates of the Immigration into Japan during the 1, 000 Year Period from 300 B.C. to A.D. 700 |url=https://www.jstage.jst.go.jp/article/ase1993/108/4/108_4_305/_article/-char/en |journal=Anthropological Science |language=en |volume=108 |issue=4 |pages=305–319 |doi=10.1537/ase.108.305 |issn= |jstor= |id= |authorlink= |accessdate=|doi-access=free }}</ref> estimating a smaller number of migrants (around 50 to 100 migrants/year).

Recently, there is a shift from finding population estimates to finding the number of waves that entered Japan, as deducing an exact number across several millennia is deemed less feasible. The waves are identified through genetics, anthropology, and linguistics.<ref name=":12">{{Cite journal |last=Wang |first=Chuan-Chao |date=2021 |title=Genomic insights into the formation of human populations in East Asia |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/349510968 |journal=Nature |volume=591 |issue=7850 |pages=413–419 |bibcode=2021Natur.591..413W |doi=10.1038/s41586-021-03336-2 |pmc=7993749 |pmid=33618348}}</ref><ref name=":03">{{Cite journal |last=Miyamoto |first=Kazuo |date=6 January 2022 |title=The emergence of 'Transeurasian' language families in Northeast Asia as viewed from archaeological evidence |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/357634119 |journal=ResearchGate |pages=25}}</ref>

== Genetics ==
The term "Toraijin" usually encompasses the [[Jōmon period]], [[Yayoi period]], [[Kofun period]], and the [[Asuka period]], therefore it is considered too broad to be condensed into a single name or a group genealogically.

For scientific analysis of the Japanese people's ancestry, see [[Genetic and anthropometric studies on Japanese people]].
